wayangAbout: Wayang Uwuh is a contemporary art and wayang practice made from recycled inorganic waste, initiated by artist Iskandar Hardjodimuljo.
wayangOrigin: Wayang Uwuh’s creative journey began in Jakarta in 2013, when Iskandar Hardjodimuljo felt deeply concerned about the growing urban waste problem and wanted to create an environmental learning medium rooted in local culture. After settling in Yogyakarta, Iskandar Hardjodimuljo continued developing the idea and established a studio and learning space for Wayang Uwuh in Kampung Sapen, Demangan, Gondokusuman District, Yogyakarta City. Etymologically, “uwuh” is a Javanese word meaning waste or refuse, so Wayang Uwuh means wayang made from discarded or previously used materials. Through an eco-art approach that brings together the preservation of traditional wayang art and ecological care, waste is not seen merely as dirty and useless residue, but is transformed into an artistic medium with aesthetic and economic value and a moral message about caring for nature.
wayangMaterials: Wayang Uwuh’s distinctive approach explores inorganic waste as the main material for creating wayang characters. In the making process, Iskandar Hardjodimuljo uses various household and light-industrial inorganic waste, such as used plastic bottles, mineral-water cups, straws, coffee or detergent wrappers, bottle caps, cardboard, used wire, and pieces of zinc and cans. The collected waste is first cleaned and sorted by texture, the natural colors of its packaging, and thickness. It is then cut, shaped, assembled, and painted to resemble traditional wayang characters such as Punakawan (clown-servant characters) and Pandawa (the Pandava brothers), as well as newly created characters. The work retains characteristic wayang ornamentation, including tatahan (traditional carved patterns) and sunggingan (traditional painted ornamentation), adapted to the flexibility of plastic and light metal.
wayangEducation: As it has developed, Wayang Uwuh has become more than a display piece or eco-friendly souvenir; it also serves as a medium for education, community empowerment, and cultural exchange. These recycled wayang figures are performed in theatre and educational programs to share waste-sorting messages with the public, school pupils, and university students. The Wayang Uwuh Studio in Kampung Sapen also regularly opens a learning space and workshops on making wayang from waste for local residents, visitors, and educational communities, encouraging creativity and awareness of independent waste management. Through its continued work and educational value, Wayang Uwuh artwork and performances have gained recognition nationally and internationally through participation in art festivals, environmental exhibitions, and cross-cultural collaborations with artists and environmental advocates from other countries.
